title: Evaluating evidence and sources
note: Weigh a claim by its evidence and its source. Ask who is speaking, what expertise and incentives they have, whether independent sources agree, and whether the claim could be checked or shown false. Our own minds bend evidence too: we favor what fits our views, recall vivid cases, and judge from survivors.

read.title: Weighing what you are told
text: Most of what we believe comes from other people: teachers, reporters, experts, friends. That is not a failure of thinking; no one can check everything firsthand. The skill is deciding whom to trust, and how far.

Start with the source. Does it have relevant expertise, and is it speaking inside its field? Does it have a stake in the answer, such as money or reputation? Was the witness in a position to know? Then look for independent corroboration. Fifty websites repeating one wire story are one source, not fifty. Professional fact-checkers read laterally: rather than studying a page closely, they open new tabs to see what others say about it.

Next, look at the evidence itself. A few vivid stories are weaker than a large, well-chosen sample. Results that others have replicated deserve more weight than a single study. A claim that no possible observation could refute, which Karl Popper called unfalsifiable, explains everything and therefore tells us little.

Finally, check yourself. We tend to notice evidence that fits what we already believe, to judge likelihood by what comes easily to mind, and to study only the winners. Naming these biases does not cure them, but it gives you a reason to look again.
